topics.topic: Accepted request-id syntax, length measurement, and minimum-form requirements
questions: Exactly which characters are accepted, and is the 128 limit measured in Unicode code points, encoded bytes or another unit?
Exactly which request-id strings are accepted or refused?
Exactly which request-id strings are accepted and how is the 128-character limit measured?
Is a short but otherwise printable nonblank request id accepted by Registry, or must its form encode a minimum amount of entropy or length?

quotes:
'Create a project', 'record a customer', 'add a room' and 'publish an
   artifact pointer' each carry a request id: an opaque value the caller
   makes, unique for every create it means as new — printable text of at most
   128 characters, made from at least 16 random bytes, as a random UUID is; a
   blank one is missing (A02).
judgement.why: This is the same request-id syntax, repertoire, equality and length-measurement question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Accepted request-id syntax, length measurement, and equality
quotes:
'Create a project', 'record a customer', 'add a room' and 'publish an
   artifact pointer' each carry a request id: an opaque value the caller
   makes, unique for every create it means as new — printable text of at most
   128 characters, made from at least 16 random bytes, as a random UUID is; a
   blank one is missing (A02).
precedent.why: The exact character repertoire, string equality and measurement unit are field-format and encoding contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Audit-erasure cutoff selected for replay after restore
questions: Is the cutoff replayed after restore the cutoff from the most recently performed erasure, or the greatest cutoff date ever applied?
After restore, should the owner replay the chronologically last audit-erasure action or the greatest cutoff date ever applied?
Which cutoff must be applied after restore when later erasure actions used an older date than an earlier action?

quotes:
What the owner repeats after a restore — erasures,
restrictions, ends of a relationship, the latest date audit entries were
erased by — follows the owner's record of the retention review (R0-60): a
governance document, outside this case (Explicit exclusions), naming each
action by its date, kind and the `customer_ref` or `project_id` it touched —
an audit erasure by its date alone — with no personal value.

The date of an erasure is a date not later than today, the current date in
   UTC; a later date is refused.

The owner first starts the restored instance owner-only (A17 rule 1), so
   no service and no agent reaches it, and brings each Customer and project to
   the state the owner's own record of the retention review (R0-60) gives for
   it now — erased, restricted, ended or not — and erases audit entries before
   the latest date the owner erased by, before configuring the tokens and
   starting it again.
judgement.divergence: One implementation replays the cutoff from the chronologically last erasure action; another applies the greatest cutoff ever used, so the owner sees different older audit entries survive after restoration.
judgement.why: The rules permit erasure cutoffs in non-monotonic order but do not define which meaning of “latest date” governs recovery.

topics.topic: Backup outcome and retention semantics when deletion or status writing fails
questions: What outcome is recorded and shown when, for example, a checked backup is kept but deletion of an expired backup fails?
Does a status-file write failure make an otherwise checked backup count as failed, is that backup kept, and when is status writing retried?
What is the run outcome in mixed-success cases, and is a successfully checked backup retained when the status file cannot be written?

quotes:
Each run writes its
   outcome and instant to a status file in the backup location, which a
   restart keeps; it is written after the backup is kept or the run fails,

Every day at the same run — whether the new backup succeeded or not —
   Registry deletes every backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before.

A backup or a deletion that fails leaves no partial file, writes a
   diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at
   the next run; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.divergence: One implementation keeps a successfully checked backup and records a mixed or deletion-failed outcome; another treats any deletion or status-write failure as failure of the whole run and may discard or not count that backup, which the owner notices in backup status and recovery availability.
judgement.why: The text requires one run outcome but does not define aggregation of independently successful and failed phases or the effect of status-file write failure.

topics.topic: Canonical encoding, ordering, and digest algorithm for confirmation-bound inputs
questions: What exact byte representation is digested so that confirmation-time inputs can be compared with the inputs originally shown?
How are confirmation-bound values canonically encoded and digested so every implementation decides equality identically?
How are confirmation-bound values canonically encoded and ordered, and which digest algorithm is used?

quotes:
kept as a digest of those values in a fixed order, never
   as the values themselves; a submission's inputs are bound when their digest
   equals it.
judgement.why: This is the same canonical encoding, ordering and digest-computation question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Canonical encoding and digest computation for confirmation-bound inputs
quotes:
kept as a digest of those values in a fixed order, never
   as the values themselves; a submission's inputs are bound when their digest
   equals it.
precedent.why: The canonical byte encoding, field order, digest algorithm and representation of absent values are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Configured-secret representation and byte-length measurement
questions: What value is measured for the 32-byte startup check?
How are owner credentials, service tokens and the backup key represented and converted to bytes for length, equality and constant-time comparison?
How is the 32-byte minimum measured for configured credentials and keys?

quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
judgement.why: The textual or binary representation, decoding, equality and byte-counting rules for credential fields are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Validation and conflict handling for records belonging to unpicked import projects
questions: Are malformed rooms and pointers belonging only to unpicked projects checked and reported, or completely ignored?
Does a room or pointer id duplicated between a picked project and an unpicked project refuse the import?
Apart from the explicitly global upload checks, can a malformed record belonging only to an unpicked project block confirmation or appear in the mapping?
Are malformations and conflicts outside the picked subset shown, ignored, or only checked when the owner picks that project?

quotes:
As the owner picks projects,
   the mapping shows for the picks only: their rooms and pointers; the display
   name and alias each will arrive under — its v1 name and no alias unless the
   owner gives others (R0-85), a name being required (A02).

and every malformed record and every id that
   conflicts with one production holds.

Registry checks what the picks bring in — each picked project with the
   rooms and pointers that name it and the v1 value it names — and nothing
   else of the file; a room or pointer naming another project belongs to that
   project: records only of projects the owner did not pick are neither checked,
   shown as conflicts nor imported, and take no part in the duplicate-id
   check.

Any conflict — a project, room or
   pointer id production holds — or any malformed record refuses the whole
   import, and nothing changes (R0-50, R0-79).
judgement.why: The mapping and confirmation rules refer without qualification to every malformed record and any malformed record, while the picked-subset rule says records of unpicked projects are not checked or shown.

topics.topic: Backup-phase continuation and ordering after cleanup or retention failures
questions: After preliminary cleanup or retention deletion fails, which remaining phases of that run still execute, and in what order?
After temporary-file cleanup fails, does the run still perform retention deletion, and what outcome is recorded if that deletion succeeds or also fails?

quotes:
A backup and its check file are
   written under temporary names in the backup location — every one beginning
   with the prefix the release declares for them — and become a kept backup
   only when complete; at every start and every run Registry first removes
   every file left there under that prefix, and no other file. A removal that fails is reported;
   the run then makes no backup and counts as failed, and the start goes on
   serving.

Every day at the same run — whether the new backup succeeded or not —
   Registry deletes every backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before.

A backup or a deletion that fails leaves no partial file, writes a
   diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at
   the next run; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.divergence: One implementation still performs retention deletion after preliminary cleanup fails and continues backup creation after an expired-backup deletion fails; another stops the remaining phases at either failure, so the owner observes different backup freshness and retention.
judgement.why: Cleanup is declared first and retention is required even when a new backup fails, but the continuation and ordering behavior around cleanup and retention failures is not fully specified.

topics.topic: Date recorded for ended relationships so restore reproduces Customer state
questions: For an end-of-relationship action, does the recorded date mean the action date or the effective relationship-end date needed to reproduce the Customer state?
For an `end relationship` record, does “its date” mean the action date, the effective relationship-end date, or must both be kept so the restored Customer can be reconstructed?

quotes:
What the owner repeats after a restore — erasures,
restrictions, ends of a relationship, the latest date audit entries were
erased by — follows the owner's record of the retention review (R0-60): a
governance document, outside this case (Explicit exclusions), naming each
action by its date, kind and the `customer_ref` or `project_id` it touched —
an audit erasure by its date alone — with no personal value.

Ending a customer relationship records the date the owner gives — the day the
relationship in fact ended, which may be earlier than the action — or today when
the owner gives none.
judgement.why: The questioned meaning is a field note in the external governance record, expressly outside this case, and therefore belongs to State 7 notes.

topics.topic: Owner-session cookie attributes, browser lifetime, HTTP behavior, and expiry
questions: What exact cookie attributes and local-HTTP behaviour enforce the stated browser boundary?
What exact cookie attributes and browser lifetime apply, and does Registry explicitly expire the cookie when the server-side session ends?

quotes:
The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner
   session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over
   HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only
   to Registry's own origin.
judgement.why: This is the same owner-session cookie attributes, scope and HTTP-behavior question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Owner-session cookie attributes and route, host, port, and HTTPS scope
quotes: The owner signs in with the owner credential (R0-30) and receives an owner session (M11), carried by a cookie that scripts cannot read, sent only over HTTPS when the interface is reached from another machine (R0-29), and only to Registry's own origin.
precedent.why: Exact cookie attributes, host/path scope and SameSite transport policy are HTTP contract and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Owner-session idle-period reference instant and concurrent-request ordering
questions: From which instant does the renewed 30-minute idle period run when an owner request takes time to complete?
At what instant is `last_request` updated, and how are concurrent ordinary owner requests ordered for idle-expiry purposes?

quotes:
An owner request is any request to the owner interface that
   carries the valid session, whatever its answer; it restarts the 30
   minutes; before the first request it runs from the sign-in.

Validity is
   checked when a request arrives (A04 rule 6, stage 1); a request that
   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).

The requests of one owner session that change its state — showing a
   confirmation step, uploading a file, a submission — are applied one at a
   time: each sees the session as the one before left it, so a confirmation
   bound to a file a later upload replaced is refused (A16 rule 2).
judgement.divergence: One implementation renews the idle deadline from request arrival and orders concurrent arrivals then; another renews it at completion, letting a long or later-completing request extend the session further, which the owner notices when a subsequent request is accepted or requires sign-in.
judgement.why: The rules define arrival-time validity and serialized state-changing requests but never define when last-request time is written or how concurrent ordinary requests affect it.

topics.topic: Reconstruction of missing or unusable backup-status information
questions: What outcome is shown after status information is lost or cannot be written, particularly after a later failure or when there are no backups?
What `last outcome` and instant are written when status is reconstructed solely from kept backups?

quotes:
Each run writes its outcome and instant to a status file in the backup
   location, which a restart keeps; it is written after the backup is kept or
   the run fails, and a status file missing, unreadable or older than the newest kept backup
   is rewritten at start from the kept backups, which alone say whether a day
   has one; the owner interface shows the newest kept backup's instant
   and that last outcome, so the owner sees when a backup holds the import
   (A16 rule 10).

A backup or a deletion that fails leaves no partial file, writes a
   diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at
   the next run; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.divergence: One implementation reconstructs the last outcome as success at the newest kept backup; another reports unknown, missing, or a synthesized failure, so the owner sees different operational status after the status file is lost, especially when a later failed run cannot be recovered.
judgement.why: Kept backups can establish successful backup instants but cannot reconstruct a later failed run, and the required replacement outcome is not defined.

topics.topic: Required backup encryption, integrity, metadata, and key-digest format
questions: What precise cryptographic format makes a backup confidential and tamper-detecting across releases?
Which cryptographic construction and metadata format must every implementation use, and how is the exposed key digest computed without enabling unsafe key verification?

quotes:
Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its
   making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
judgement.why: This is the same backup cryptographic construction, authenticated envelope and metadata-format question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Required backup encryption construction and interoperable envelope format
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Temporary backup naming, cleanup eligibility, and partial-file handling
questions: May a failed backup or failed cleanup leave a temporary partial file in the backup location?
Which exact names are temporary and cleanup-eligible, and how are kept backups distinguished so cleanup cannot delete them?

quotes:
A backup and its check file are
   written under temporary names in the backup location — every one beginning
   with the prefix the release declares for them — and become a kept backup
   only when complete; at every start and every run Registry first removes
   every file left there under that prefix, and no other file. A removal that fails is reported;
   the run then makes no backup and counts as failed, and the start goes on
   serving.

A backup or a deletion that fails leaves no partial file, writes a
   diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at
   the next run; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.divergence: One implementation leaves an unremovable temporary partial file for the next cleanup and gives kept backups names outside the cleanup prefix; another interprets the no-partial-file rule as requiring immediate cleanup or may leave final backups under the prefix, changing whether a later start deletes data the owner expected to retain.
judgement.why: The rules do not reconcile failed temporary-file removal with the no-partial-file statement or state how a completed backup ceases to match the cleanup prefix.

topics.topic: Whether an import-triggered backup satisfies the daily backup requirement
questions: Does an import-triggered backup count as that day's ordinary backup, especially when it occurs before 03:00 UTC?
Does an import-triggered backup count as that day’s ordinary backup and suppress the scheduled/startup daily backup?

quotes:
A run that 03:00 found Registry stopped is made when
   it next starts with its service tokens, if no backup was made that UTC
   day; an owner-only start makes no run (rule 10).

The run after an accepted import (A16)
   is made even when the day already has a backup, and keeps both; besides
   it, at most one backup is made per UTC day, the kept backups themselves
   saying which days have one, and runs never overlap.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats an import-triggered backup as the day's backup and suppresses the scheduled or startup run; another treats it as additional and still makes one ordinary daily backup, so the owner observes a different number and timing of recoverable backups.
judgement.why: The text makes the import run additional when a daily backup already exists but does not say whether an earlier import run satisfies the ordinary daily requirement.
